children: By Junko Fujita
Markets are repricing the Bank of Japan's interest rate hike path next year on a possible slowdown in AI-driven spending and as falling commodity prices soften inflationary pressures.

The yield curve of Japanese government bonds is steepening, while the break-even inflation rate (JPBEI10Y=RR), the yield gap between 10-year JGBs and 10-year inflation-linked bonds, is at the lowest since mid-February.
Growing concerns about the AI trade have buffeted global stocks and added pressure on Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's plan for economic growth, which relies heavily on technology investment.

The BOJ is still widely expected to raise its key policy rate for the third time this year at its December meeting as it tries to contain above-target inflation and support the yen. But the market is growing less sure about the speed and extent of increases beyond that.

"There is a growing view that inflation can be curbed without raising interest rates," said Katsutoshi Inadome, senior strategist at Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Asset Management. "If AI investments slow down, the economy could cool off and inflation may stop rising."
SHIFT IN MARKET THINKING

Accelerating inflation and a weaker yen had traders expecting the BOJ to step up the pace of its policy tightening, with the benchmark 10-year JGB yield rising to a 30-year high of 3.115% in September.
Such expectations were strengthened when US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pressured BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda to raise interest rates.

That trend has since largely reversed. The 10-year JGB yield fell to as low as 2.61% in early November. The 5-year JGB yield fell to 2.025% earlier this month from a record high of 2.43% in September.

The shift has been driven by concerns that AI investment may slow in the United States after Democrats swept the midterm elections, raising expectations that Democrats may impose tougher regulations on the industry. Any slowdown could affect demand for chips and other related needs such as electricity, putting pressure on the economy.
As well, energy prices have fallen this month even though the Middle East conflict remains unresolved. Brent crude futures
are down about 24% from their recent peak on October 30.

The 1-month swap rate starting in two years (JPYSB6L2YF1M=), which market players see as the end point of the BOJ's tightening cycle, rose to a record high of 2.5% in September, after Bessent pressed for a rate hike. That swap rate was down to 1.926% on Wednesday, the lowest since July 23.
BOJ EXPECTED TO RAISE RATES IN DECEMBER

With the yen stuck near 160 per dollar, a level that has been a trigger for intervention, economists polled by Reuters expect the BOJ to raise its policy rate by 25 basis points to 1.5% at its December policy meeting.

"The view for the next year's rate path is divided, with some expecting the BOJ to end the rate-hike cycle in March at 1.75%, with others betting the rate to rise to 2% in June," said Takashi Fujiwara, lead fund manager at Resona Asset Management. "Now bets are converging at 1.75%."

Markets are pricing in at least two more hikes by the US Federal Reserve. That means the gap to US rates, which has been a weight on the yen, could widen if the Fed moves more aggressively to contain inflation.
